Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Minh was sixty-two when it happened, though he still remembers every second with a clarity that feels like a curse. He had been a roofer for forty years—since he came to this country from Vietnam as a young man—and he knew the work, knew the heat of tar and the sting of solvents. That morning he was sealing a flat commercial roof, the kind of job he had done a thousand times. A wind caught a spray of sealant and drove it straight into his face before he could turn away. The chemical burned his eyes and throat instantly, and he felt his chest seize as if a hand had closed around his lungs. He collapsed on the roof, gasping, and his foreman called 911. The next thing Minh knew was a fluorescent ceiling in the ICU, a tube down his throat, and the sharp, clean smell of antiseptic that he now cannot stand even for a moment.

In the months that followed, Minh tried to go back to work, but something had shifted. The memory of that day played like a film he could not stop—the sudden sting, the panic of not being able to breathe, the sirens. Sometimes the feeling returned without any image at all: a wave of terror would wash over him while he was just sitting at the dinner table, his heart pounding for no reason he could name. He began to notice that he could no longer relax, even at home with the door locked and his wife Lien beside him. His body stayed tight, waiting. He had trouble concentrating on simple tasks—measuring shingles, counting tiles—and his boss noticed that Minh started making mistakes he never made before. Minh came to believe that he could not rely on himself anymore. If his own body had betrayed him on a routine job, how could he trust his judgment about anything?

The triggers multiplied. The darkness of early morning when he woke before dawn became unbearable; he associated it with the dim ICU room where he had lain helpless. Any hospital smell—even a bandage or a doctor’s waiting room—sent a jolt through him. And related smells, like bleach or paint thinner, made him gag and turn away. He started refusing jobs that required chemical sealants, then jobs on unfamiliar roofs where he could not predict the dangers. Eventually he stopped taking any new projects at all, sticking only to the handful of houses he had worked on for years. His income dropped, and he felt shame piling on top of fear.

At home, Minh changed too. He used to argue with Lien about small things—money, chores—but after the exposure he stopped disagreeing altogether. He had become convinced that conflict was dangerous, that any confrontation could somehow trigger another catastrophe. So he nodded when Lien complained, said nothing when she made plans he did not like. She began to feel that he had disappeared into himself. Minh tried hard not to think about the trauma, but the film kept playing, and the feelings kept rising without warning. The world felt like a dangerous place now, not just the roof but everywhere; he avoided unfamiliar streets, unfamiliar faces, because he could not tell what might go wrong. He dwelled on who he used to be—a steady, capable man who could handle anything—and the gap between that man and the man he had become felt like a chasm he would never cross.

What finally brought Minh to a clinic was Lien’s insistence, but also his own quiet despair. He had started to feel that there was no future worth planning for. At sixty-six, he thought, maybe this was just what old age felt like. But Lien told him it was not like that before, and she was right. He came because a part of him still hoped—though he was afraid to say it—that he could find a way to stop the film, to let his shoulders drop, to sit in the dark without his heart racing. He wanted to be able to disagree with his wife again, to take a new job without scanning the horizon for what might kill him. He was not sure he believed it was possible, but he showed up anyway, and that was the first step.
